title: Two Sum II — Input Array Is Sorted
directAnswer: The array is sorted — that single fact kills the hash map. Put one pointer at each end and look at the sum: if it's too big, move the right pointer left; if it's too small, move the left pointer right. O(n) time, O(1) space. Return 1-indexed positions, not 0-indexed.

remember.pattern: Opposite-end two pointers on a sorted array
remember.formula:
lo, hi = 0, n - 1
while lo < hi:
    s = nums[lo] + nums[hi]
    if s == target: return [lo + 1, hi + 1]   # 1-indexed!
    elif s < target: lo += 1   # need bigger → move left pointer right
    else: hi -= 1              # need smaller → move right pointer left
rules: Return **1-indexed** positions — `[lo + 1, hi + 1]`. This is the #1 wrong-answer on this exact problem.
Sum **too small** → move `lo` right (toward larger values). Sum **too big** → move `hi` left (toward smaller values). Never both.
Loop while `lo < hi`, never `lo <= hi` — equal pointers would reuse one element twice.
The sorted order is the **whole point** — it makes each comparison tell you which pointer to move. Do **not** reach for a hash map here.
No extra space, no sorting cost — the input is already sorted, so this is strictly better than Two Sum's hash map.
whenToUse: Array (or string) is **sorted** and you need a pair summing to a target
You want **O(1) space** — no room for a hash map
Each comparison can tell you which side to discard / advance
Monotonic structure: moving a pointer changes the sum predictably
antiSignals: Array is **unsorted** and you need original indices → hash map (classic Two Sum)
Sorting would destroy a required index mapping → don't sort, use a hash map
You need **all** pairs, not one → fix-one + two-pointer (3Sum) or counting
Lookups aren't monotonic in a pointer's position → two pointers won't converge
remember.takeaway: When an array is sorted, opposite-end two pointers turn pair-finding into an O(n)/O(1) sweep: the sign of (sum − target) tells you exactly which pointer to move. This is the same engine inside 3Sum, Container With Most Water, and Trapping Rain Water.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you exploit the 'sorted' precondition instead of blindly reusing the Two Sum hash map. The whole problem is a one-word change ('sorted') that should change your entire approach.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Returning 0-indexed answers (the prompt demands 1-indexed), or reaching for a hash map and throwing away the O(1)-space win the sorted input hands you for free.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Say out loud: 'Because it's sorted, I can converge two pointers from the ends in O(1) space — strictly better than the hash map I'd use for unsorted Two Sum.' Then justify *why* moving each pointer is correct.

problemStatement:
Given a **1-indexed** array of integers `numbers` that is already sorted in non-decreasing order, find two numbers such that they add up to a specific `target`.

Return the indices of the two numbers, `index1` and `index2`, **added by one** as an integer array `[index1, index2]` of length 2, where `1 ≤ index1 < index2 ≤ numbers.length`.

The tests are generated such that there is ***exactly one solution***. You may not use the same element twice. Your solution must use only **constant extra space**.
constraints: numbers is sorted in non-decreasing order
understanding: It's Two Sum with two twists: the array is already sorted, and the answer must be 1-indexed. The sorted guarantee unlocks an O(1)-space two-pointer sweep, and the constant-space requirement explicitly forbids the hash-map approach you'd use for unsorted Two Sum.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the array guaranteed sorted, and in which order?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — non-decreasing. That precondition is the entire reason two pointers works; without it you'd be back to a hash map.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are the returned indices 0-indexed or 1-indexed?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: 1-indexed. The prompt says 'added by one'. Returning [lo, hi] instead of [lo + 1, hi + 1] is the most common silent failure.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is there always exactly one solution?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. So I can return immediately on the first matching pair without worrying about ties.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the values be negative or duplicated?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Both. Negatives are fine — the comparison logic doesn't assume positivity. Duplicates are fine too because lo < hi guarantees two distinct positions.

examples.explanation: -1 + 0 = -1. Negatives work with no special handling.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Nested Pair Scan
approaches.whenToMention: Mention briefly to anchor the progression, then immediately note it ignores the 'sorted' gift and is strictly worse.
hints: Forget the sorted property for a moment. What's the most literal way to find a pair that sums to target?
Try every pair (i, j) with j > i and test numbers[i] + numbers[j] == target.
Two nested loops; return [i + 1, j + 1] on the first match. Note: this wastes the sorted order entirely.
approaches.complexityReasoning: n(n−1)/2 ≈ n²/2 comparisons in the worst case; no extra data structures, so O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
The mechanical translation of the prompt: fix the first index `i`, sweep every later index `j`, and check whether the two values add to `target`. Return the 1-indexed pair on the first hit.

**Why mention it at all.** Even though it's quadratic, stating it shows you derive the optimal from a baseline rather than memorizing. It also lets you contrast: 'this works on *any* array, sorted or not — which is exactly why it's wasteful here.'

**Why it throws away the key fact.** The problem went out of its way to tell you the array is **sorted**. Brute force never reads that signal — it would run identically on a shuffled array. Any time the interviewer hands you a precondition and your algorithm ignores it, you're leaving the intended solution on the table.

**Why we don't ship it.** With `n` up to `3 × 10⁴`, `n²/2` is ~450 million comparisons — borderline and pointless when the sorted structure gives you a linear sweep for free. State it, name its cost, and pivot to two pointers in the same breath.
approaches.insight: Brute force is precondition-blind: it would behave the same on an unsorted array. The moment you notice your candidate solution doesn't use a stated property ('sorted'), that's your cue a better algorithm exists.

approaches.name: Opposite-End Two Pointers (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Lead with 'because it's sorted' — that justification is the whole point of the medium rating.
hints: The array is sorted. If you stand one pointer at the smallest value and one at the largest, what does their sum tell you about which value to swap out?
If the sum is too big, the only way to shrink it without losing reachable pairs is to move the right pointer left. If it's too small, move the left pointer right.
Loop while lo < hi. On equality return [lo + 1, hi + 1]. Each step discards exactly one element that can't be part of any answer — that's why it's O(n).
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each iteration moves lo right or hi left by one, so the pointers meet after at most n − 1 steps → O(n) time. Two integer indices only → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
Place `lo` at index `0` (smallest value) and `hi` at index `n − 1` (largest value). Compute `sum = numbers[lo] + numbers[hi]`. If it equals `target`, return `[lo + 1, hi + 1]`. If it's less than `target`, advance `lo`; if greater, retreat `hi`. Repeat while `lo < hi`.

**Why moving a pointer is provably safe.** Suppose `sum > target`. Because the array is sorted, `numbers[hi]` is the **largest** value still in play. Pairing it with anything to its left gives a sum `≥ sum` only if we picked a *larger* left value — but the smallest possible partner for `numbers[hi]` is `numbers[lo]`, and even *that* overshoots. So `numbers[hi]` can never be part of a valid pair, and we can discard it forever by doing `hi--`. The symmetric argument holds for `sum < target`: `numbers[lo]` is too small to ever reach the target even paired with the maximum, so we drop it with `lo++`. **Every step eliminates exactly one element that is provably useless** — this elimination argument is the heart of the proof and what you should say aloud.

**Why this beats the hash map here.** Classic Two Sum uses `O(n)` extra space because the array is unsorted — you must *remember* what you've seen. Here the sorted order means each comparison already tells you which direction to go, so you carry **no memory at all**: two integer indices. The problem even mandates `O(1)` space, explicitly ruling the hash map out. Sorted input plus a target comparison is the canonical two-pointer setup.

**Why `lo < hi` and not `lo <= hi`.** The two numbers must occupy *distinct* positions. If we allowed `lo == hi`, we'd be adding one element to itself, which violates 'may not use the same element twice'. Stopping the moment the pointers meet guarantees `index1 < index2` always holds.

**Why the single-solution guarantee matters.** Because exactly one pair works, the first equality we hit is *the* answer — no need to keep scanning. If the problem asked for all pairs, we'd skip past duplicates on both ends after recording a hit instead of returning.
approaches.insight: The sign of `(sum − target)` is a compass: positive means 'too big, shrink from the right'; negative means 'too small, grow from the left'. Each comparison deletes one candidate permanently, so a quadratic pair search collapses into a single linear pass with zero extra memory. Internalize this and 3Sum, Container With Most Water, and Trapping Rain Water all become variations on the same converging-pointers idea.

pitfalls: Returning [lo, hi] instead of [lo + 1, hi + 1] — the problem is 1-indexed.
Using lo <= hi — lets a single element pair with itself.
Moving the wrong pointer (e.g. lo-- when sum is too big) — the pointers never converge.
Reaching for a hash map and violating the O(1)-space requirement.

commonMistakes: Using a hash map and ignoring the mandated O(1) space.
Looping with lo <= hi, allowing an element to pair with itself.
Moving the wrong pointer so the sum diverges from the target.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: 0-indexed instead of 1-indexed return
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The prompt explicitly says the indices are 'added by one'. Returning the raw pointers fails every test even though the logic is correct.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Moving the wrong pointer
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If you advance lo when the sum is too big, you only make the sum larger — the pointers diverge and never find the answer.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Reusing one element via lo <= hi
commonMistakesDetailed.why: When lo == hi the loop adds numbers[lo] to itself, which can produce a false match and violates 'may not use the same element twice'.
